lesson.title: Putting Words on Disk: The write() Method
lesson.summary: The write() method sends a string to an open file at its current position and returns the number of characters written, but unlike print() it never adds a newline for you, and it only works on a file opened in a writable mode.
lesson.body:
Writing to a file uses the mirror image method of `read()`: `file.write(some_string)`. It sends exactly the characters in `some_string` to the file at its current position, nothing more and nothing less. That "exactly" matters, because unlike `print()`, `write()` does not add a newline character for you. If you want the next thing you write to land on a new line, you have to include `"\n"` in the string yourself. Forgetting this is one of the most common surprises when someone switches from `print()` to `write()` for the first time.

For `write()` to work at all, the file has to be open in a mode that permits writing, `"w"`, `"a"`, or `"x"`, not the default `"r"`. This connects directly back to file modes: opening a file for reading only and then trying to write to it does not silently fail, it raises an error, because Python checks whether the file object supports writing before it lets you attempt it.

```python
file = open("diary.txt", "w")
count = file.write("Dear diary,")
file.write(" today I learned about files.")
print(count)
file.close()

file = open("diary.txt", "r")
print(file.read())
file.close()
```

```python
11
Dear diary, today I learned about files.
```

`write()` also returns a value: the number of characters it wrote. `"Dear diary,"` is eleven characters long, so `count` is `11`. The second call to `write()` appends `" today I learned about files."` right after the first, with no automatic newline or space added between them, which is exactly why that leading space was typed in by hand. Reading the file back afterward shows both pieces joined into one continuous sentence, because that is genuinely all that was ever written to disk.

Now see what happens when the mode does not allow writing at all.

```python
import io

file = open("diary.txt", "r")
try:
    file.write("oops")
except io.UnsupportedOperation as error:
    print("Error:", error)
file.close()
```

```python
Error: not writable
```

Opening `"diary.txt"` in `"r"` mode gives back a file object that only supports reading, so calling `.write()` on it raises `io.UnsupportedOperation`, with the message `"not writable"`, instead of quietly doing nothing or corrupting the file. Wrapping it in `try` and `except` here just demonstrates the error cleanly, but the real lesson is to reach for `write()` only after opening a file in a mode built for it.
